hook: A student in Chicago is saving for a summer in Spain. The rent there is set in euros, but her savings are in dollars, so one number decides how far her money goes: how many dollars it takes to buy one euro. When that number moves, her summer gets cheaper or dearer without any price in Spain changing.

prereq.q: A US tourist pays for a hotel in Spain. How does the balance of payments record it?
options: As an import of services, a debit in the US current account
As a credit in the US capital and financial account
As an export of services by the United States
It is not recorded, since no asset is bought
prereq.why: Money leaves the US to pay for a service bought abroad: an import of services, a current account debit.

prereq.q: Which function of money lets you compare the prices of two things, such as a jacket and a phone?
prereq.why: A unit of account is a common measure of value. An exchange rate lets you compare prices set in two different units.

figure.caption: One rate written two ways (1.25 dollars per euro is 0.80 euro per dollar). When a euro buys more dollars, the euro appreciates and the dollar depreciates.

chain.cause: The price of a euro rises from 1.25 dollars to 1.50 dollars
chain.effect: each euro buys more dollars: the euro appreciates
each dollar buys fewer euros (0.80 to about 0.67): the dollar depreciates

chain.cause: The dollar depreciates against the euro
chain.effect: goods priced in euros cost Americans more dollars, and goods priced in dollars cost Europeans fewer euros

ideas: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in units of another: "1.25 dollars per euro" is the price of one euro.
The same rate can be written either way; one quote is the reciprocal of the other: 1.25 dollars per euro is $\frac{1}{1.25} = 0.80$ euro per dollar.
A currency appreciates when one unit buys more of the other currency, and depreciates when it buys less. When one currency appreciates, the other depreciates.
To convert a price, multiply it by a rate whose units cancel: euros times dollars per euro gives dollars.

misconception.wrong: A bigger number in an exchange rate quote always means that currency got stronger.
misconception.right: It depends on the units. In "dollars per euro", a bigger number means the euro appreciated and the dollar depreciated. Flip the quote to euros per dollar and the same change makes the number smaller.

summary: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another, and it can be written two ways that are reciprocals of each other. When one unit of a currency buys more of the other currency, it has appreciated, and the other has depreciated by the same change. Read the units before you compare two rates or convert a price: the units tell you which currency the number is the price of.
